newsitem.title: UK: Economists say sterling to put further squeeze on profits.
newsitem.headline: Economists say sterling to put further squeeze on profits.

text.p: British companies are complaining about the strength of the pound as it squeezes their profits, but economists say the worst may be yet to come.
Even though official figures for Britain's trade balance are not yet showing the damage, they will soon.

The latest corporate giant to suffer from sterling's stellar rise was British Steel Plc. This week it reported a collapse in annual profits, down to 451 million pounds ($735.9 million) from 1.1 billion the year before.
The dive in earnings will force it to cut jobs and put the squeeze on suppliers -- mainly because the pound has eaten so far into margins.
Sterling has risen no less than 19 percent against a basket of major currencies since last August. As it climbs, so do British exporters' prices abroad.
Sir Brian Moffat, British Steel's chairman and chief executive, said its problems were not over despite brightening prospects in the steel market.

"The strength of sterling is a problem to British Steel and to many of its U.K. customers who are also significant exporters. Their order books are bound to be affected later this year if sterling remains at its present level," he said.
SMALLER COMPANIES SUFFER TOO
When a big fish like British Steel suffers, so do all the minnows who rely on it.
Richard Jeffrey, group economist at Charterhouse Tilney, said the pain inflicted by the pound was sharpest in so-called intermediate industries, like steel.

"The harder it is to differentiate your product, the more relative volumes are directly related to price," he said. "In areas like consumer and capital goods, pricing pressures have not been so severe and export volumes are actually still growing."
Consumer goods companies find it much easier to entice customers with extra add-ons or incentives to buy the basic product. But steel is simply steel. Price is everything.

Even if that were not so, companies which sell mainly on Britain's high streets are encountering near-boom conditions as consumers spend freely, buoyed partly by billions of pounds of shares given away by building societies converting into banks.

Retail sales jumped 1.1 percent in May and were 1.8 percent higher in the latest three months than the previous three -- the highest quarterly rate of growth since 1988, when Britain was in the middle of a major boom.

But manufacturers who rely more on foreign markets have not been able to join in the fun, blighted by a combination of weak continental European markets and a currency that constantly forces their prices up.
And it is not only secondary industries that are suffering. Computer firm Psion Plc said this week that its performance was also being hit by the pound.

Late last month, the Confederation of British Industry -- Britain's top employers' organisation -- said export demand was at its lowest level since November 1993. However, buoyant domestic conditions were offsetting export weakness.

Official trade figures have held up well, despite the strength of sterling. In March, Britain's global trade deficit was 671 million pounds, well below the 1.1 billion gap in March last year. Total exports were almost exactly the same.
"Margin has been sacrificed by manufacturers with the objective of protecting volumes," Jeffrey said. But unless the pound declines soon, it is only a matter of time until the trade gap worsens.
"We are going to see slower growth in exports. We are still working through the J-curve," he said.
The J-curve describes the way in which an appreciating currency is of short term benefit to a country's terms of trade. Prices change immediately but trading partners are slower to react.
But once they do fight shy of the rise in prices, the J-curve unwinds and the balance of trade deteriorates despite attempts by exporters to protect market share.
Andrew Sentance, director of the London Business School's Centre for Economic Forecasting, said sterling's full force would not be felt until next year.
"The full impact depends on how quickly the pound returns to a more normal level around 2.40 to 2.50 marks ($1.44)," he said. "We don't see that happening this year."
Since last August, the pound has shot up from around 2.27 marks to 2.84 -- its highest level in nearly five years.
"I think we will see a deterioration in the trade balance over the second half of the year with the full effects being seen over 1998 as a whole."
He forecast a current account deficit of 8.8 billion stg next year. A recent poll of independent experts by Britain's Treasury found a consensus forecasting a deficit of 4.3 billion this year.
Sentance agreed with Jeffrey that manufacturers had taken some of the pressure on their profit margins.

Others have protected themselves against violent currency movements by hedging -- buying the pound forward at an agreed price months in advance or buying currency options to offset exposure. But that cannot last forever.
"Hedging certainly helps for a while but will catch up with you eventually," Sentance said. Most companies only hedge for a number of months or perhaps a year.
If the pound retains its powerful position after that, then they will have to pay the price.
But all is not doom and gloom for manufacturers.

Sentance said the strength of domestic demand would bail them out to a large extent and the official figures bear him out. Manufacturing output jumped 0.6 percent in April and was up 2.3 percent on a year ago, despite the squeeze on exports.

But more than that, Sentance said there were signs of life from continental Europe, where economies have had to withstand austerity tax and spending policies as governments prepare for a single European currency.
"There is some evidence of European markets picking up a little, which will take some of the edge off the pound's effect," he said. ($ = 0.612 British Pounds) ($ = 1.728 German Marks)
